items.title: Territorial Acknowledgement
notes: Mayor McCabe opened the meeting with the following Territorial Acknowledgement:

We would like to begin by acknowledging that the land on which we are gathering from today is the land traditionally cared for by the Haudenosaunee, Anishnaabe and Neutral People. We also acknowledge the enduring presence and deep traditional knowledge and philosophies of the Indigenous People with whom we share their land today.

items.title: Moment of Reflection
notes: Mayor McCabe provided Council with a moment of reflection.
Today, we pause to reflect on the ongoing harmful impacts of gender-based violence in our own community and around the world.

We especially remember trans people all over the world whose lives have been lost due to anti-trans violence. November 20 was Transgender Day of Remembrance – a day of mourning and solidarity with trans people in our community whose lives are deeply affected by widespread violence. The recent Club Q murders in Colorado were a stark reminder of deadly violence affecting far too many in 2SLGBTQ+ communities.
The 16 Days of Activism Against Gender-Based Violence, observed worldwide from November 25 to December 10, is time dedicated to changing this reality.

Violence happens on a continuum, therefore our responses must reflect this – we can all take action. As a council and as a community, we must respect the right for self-determination. Upholding welcoming work places and community spaces – where we use peoples’ preferred pronouns, and support people in using any washroom of their choice are two simple ways we can actualize support. We must commit to including trans women, trans men, non-binary, Two Spirit people, gender-fluid, gender non-conforming and gender-diverse folks in conversations about women’s rights, feminism and gender equality. Ideologies that refuse to recognize trans women are harmful and further oppress trans and gender diverse people.

Let’s use this time to re-commit ourselves to a world that challenges traditionally rigid gender norms so that trans and gender diverse people can live authentically and with safety that everyone deserves.
Mayor McCabe read a second Council Statement in recognition and remembrance of the National Day of Remembrance and Action on Violence Against Women.

During the 16 Days of Activism, Canadians reflect on the presence of gender based violence in our own country. Tomorrow, on December 6, many in our community and across Canada will pause to remember the 14 young women murdered at Polytechnique Montreal and all women who have suffered gender- based violence.

These days of remembrance and activism push us to consider the links the between sexism, transphobia and homophobia, and the greater risks faced by women, trans people, non-binary people and gender-diverse people. The additional impact of racism and colonialism put Indigenous women, girls and Two Spirit people at even greater risk, similarly the impact of ableism on women with disabilities.

As a City, we recognize the importance of taking action on the devastating impacts of gender-based violence. We are also mindful that challenging sexist and transphobic systems must not be limited to a few observances throughout the year but an ongoing action.
I would now invite Councillor Freeman to make a few personal remarks regarding this day.
Councillor Freeman also shared personal remarks about the National Day of Remembrance and Action on Violence Against Women.

December 6th is a really profound date for me as a woman engineer. I was born in 1967 and I would just like to name the women who were gunned down and their ages and the academic pursuits that they were following:

• Geneviève Bergeron, born 1968, civil engineering student • Hélène Colgan, born 1966, mechanical engineering student • Nathalie Croteau, born 1966, mechanical engineering student • Barbara Daigneault, born 1967, mechanical engineering student • Anne-Marie Edward, born 1968, chemical engineering student • Maud Haviernick, born 1960, materials engineering student • Maryse Laganière, born 1964, budget clerk in the École Polytechnique's finance department

• Maryse Leclair, born 1966, materials engineering student • Anne-Marie Lemay, born 1967, mechanical engineering student • Sonia Pelletier, born 1961, mechanical engineering student • Michèle Richard, born 1968, materials engineering student • Annie St-Arneault, born 1966, mechanical engineering student • Annie Turcotte, born 1969, materials engineering student • Barbara Klucznik-Widajewicz, born 1958, nursing student On December 6th, I was working on a construction site as a Civil Engineering student, the same age as these women, and it was a very difficult day. I hadn’t heard the news. The phone in the construction trailer where I was working rang incessantly all day long with people asking if I was okay, because there was worry, more broadly, for women engineering students across the country that there could be others who would feel similarly compelled as Mr. Lépine in his desire to remove women from non-traditional careers.

I think that one of the things about this day too is it profoundly affected women choosing to enter careers in Mathematics, Sciences, and Engineering, because they felt that this could happen again. Engineering had been on a steady increase with women entering the profession in undergraduates and was near 22%, and after this shooting it dropped back to almost 10%. Here we are all these many years later and we’re only at 20%. So the recovery of women choosing careers in engineering has been profoundly impacted in the events of this day. And that’s just one of many professions where women strive to work in non-traditional careers.
This day, December 6th, is one of those days where we should pause and reflect about that struggle and how we can help to make a difference.

items.title: Questions
notes: Councillor Bodaly asked a question about the financial implications of Bill 23 as part of the next budget process, specifically about the lost revenue from Development Charges. Tim Anderson responded to Councillor Bodaly, noting that Bill 23 is really impactful to municipalities across Ontario, and that the City did submit comments to the province by the November 24th deadline. He noted that the legislation was approved, and that the City needs to adapt going forward, commenting that a report would be coming out next week detailing that adaptation plan. Filipa Reynolds also responded, noting the loss of revenue from Development Charges range from $23-$31 million dollars over the first five years, and that it doesn’t take into account operating impacts.
The capital dollars are to build infrastructure. They have paused the work on the DC Background Study and by-law.

Councillor Freeman also asked about the reserve funding, and the timing of getting a message to the province before the provincial government goes on break. Mayor McCabe offered some background on what the City is doing, as well as the Ontario Big City Mayors. Tim Anderson responded regarding the reserve fund report coming next week.

items.title: New Business
notes: Mayor McCabe offered a welcome to Filipa Reynolds in her first meeting as Commissioner of Corporate Services.

Mayor McCabe also shouted out the BIA for their tree-lighting ceremony on Friday, December 2nd, where she was joined by Coucillors Wright, Bodaly, and Roe. The Wonders of Winter started in Waterloo Park, and the park is lit up. There’s a Free Skate by the KW Lions Club happening on December 18th at RIM Park. Also on December 18th, the Menorah will be lit in the Uptown Square.

Councillor Vasic mentioned that MT Space had their last production of The Last 15 Seconds on December 1st. They are currently raising money for a bursary in director Majdi Bou-Matar’s name, which offers financial support as well as mentorship from MT Space to a newcomer, immigrant, and emerging artist each year. She also mentioned a production from Green Light Arts, as well as The Addams Family Musical put on by K-W Musical Productions. Arts and Culture is struggling, and people should go see some local theatre production.
